summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws in the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded the position publicly, stating that "there is nothing we can do." The decriminalisation arrived by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly.

The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, including its 2025 single-sex-services code, does not automatically apply in the British Virgin Islands. The territory stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume the Equality Act's discrimination and service-access protections are available there by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Family status remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid under British Virgin Islands law was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not itself a ruling on whether such a marriage is recognised in the territory.
tangentialFactors:
GlobalGayz (August 2012, updated 2017) rates the British Virgin Islands among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean, while describing native homophobia there as "silent and invisible" and gay life as lived in secret. That account describes social climate rather than law, and it suggests a gap between formal legality and everyday discretion that a trans visitor may also experience.

The decriminalisation of same-sex intimacy was imposed by the United Kingdom's Privy Council after the local House of Assembly declined to legislate, which indicates a local legislature less receptive than the imposed outcome might suggest. The Forbes-Lettsome marriage litigation, in which the BVI Christian Council intervened and sought to appeal, shows organised religious opposition actively contesting family recognition in the courts.
localsOnly:
Residents gained decriminalisation through an external judicial order rather than through their own representatives, and the public response of legislator Orlando Smith framed the change as having no local remedy. The BVI Christian Council's pursuit of appeals in the Forbes-Lettsome case indicates that local religious bodies continue to litigate against recognition of foreign same-sex marriages, with implications for residents' family formation.

Protection against discrimination for residents rests on British Virgin Islands legislation, not on the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, unless a specific Order in Council extends it. Residents seeking to rely on United Kingdom equality protections must first establish whether such an extension order exists for the territory.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Forbes-Lettsome proceedings are recorded here only up to 29 July 2022, when the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal Justice Adrian Jack's case-management orders. The subsequent course and outcome of the case, and whether any ruling on recognition of the United Kingdom same-sex marriage has since issued, are unresolved in the available sources.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, marker changes on documents, screening or identification procedures at entry, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and bathroom rules in the British Virgin Islands. Whether British Virgin Islands legislation provides any statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity is likewise not sourced here and should be verified against local statute.

Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 has ever been extended to the British Virgin Islands by Order in Council, in whole or in part, is not established by the available sources; the inventory states only that it does not apply automatically.
